title: Performance, Rendering & Instruments
scopeHtml: Scope: SwiftUI diffing and invalidation, main thread hangs, scrolling performance, image loading, memory, Instruments, launch time.

notes.title: Baseline and how iOS performance work differs
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android you profile with Android Studio Profiler, Perfetto/System Tracing, Macrobenchmark, Baseline Profiles and Play Console vitals. In iOS the same jobs are done by Instruments, Xcode Organizer, MetricKit and os_signpost.

This track assumes Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials, using @Observable, NavigationStack, async/await and Swift Testing. Legacy forms (ObservableObject/@Published, NavigationView, XCTest, Combine) appear only as "old codebases" notes.

The performance targets are physical:

  • A 60 Hz screen gives about 16.7 ms per frame; ProMotion devices run up to 120 Hz, giving about 8.3 ms. Miss the deadline and you get a hitch (a visible stutter).
  • The main thread does input, SwiftUI body evaluation, layout and commit to the render server. Heavy work there causes hangs (Apple's term for unresponsiveness; Xcode Organizer and Instruments classify main-thread stalls above roughly 250 ms as hangs, shorter ones as microhangs; verify thresholds in current docs).
  • Rendering (rasterising, compositing) happens in a separate render server process, so smooth animations survive some main-thread work but not all.
  • The OS enforces watchdog limits: an app that does not finish launching quickly enough is killed (crash code 0x8badf00d, "ate bad food").

Mapping:

Android iOS
Android Studio CPU Profiler / Perfetto Instruments Time Profiler, System Trace
Memory Profiler, LeakCanary Instruments Allocations/Leaks, Debug Memory Graph
Jank stats, Play Vitals Xcode Organizer, MetricKit
Macrobenchmark XCTMetric performance tests (XCTest), measure blocks
StrictMode Main Thread Checker, Thread Sanitizer
Baseline Profiles No direct equal; AOT-compiled native code already, so launch focuses on dyld and static initialisers
Layout Inspector Xcode View Debugger, SwiftUI instrument

Real industry examples. Meta, Uber and Airbnb publish launch-time and hitch-rate metrics as app-level SLOs; Airbnb and LinkedIn engineering blogs describe tracking scroll hitches in production with MetricKit-style data.

Analogy. A restaurant kitchen with a strict order ticket time: the main thread is the single head chef, and every extra task given to the chef delays plates reaching customers.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "iOS has no GC so it is always faster". ARC traffic, retain/release atomics and main-thread blocking still hurt.
  • Optimising without measuring; interviewers expect "profile in Instruments on a real device in Release build".
  • Android vs iOS: assuming debug builds are representative. Debug Swift can be many times slower than Release because of unoptimised generics and no inlining.

notes.title: How SwiftUI re-evaluates body and why invalidation matters
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Compose, recomposition skips composables whose inputs are stable and unchanged. SwiftUI is similar in spirit: a view's body runs again when a dependency it read changes, and SwiftUI then diffs the resulting view tree.

The model:

  1. Views are lightweight value types (structs). Creating them is cheap; they are descriptions, not the rendered objects.
  2. SwiftUI keeps a persistent attribute graph (a dependency graph) per view hierarchy. Each body is a node that reads state; when state changes, dependent nodes are marked dirty.
  3. On the next update, SwiftUI calls body for dirty views, compares the new child descriptions with the previous ones using identity and (for some inputs) value equality, and updates only the underlying render nodes that changed.
  4. With @Observable (iOS 17+), SwiftUI tracks which properties of an observable object each body actually read. Only views that read the changed property are invalidated.
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@Observable
final class CartModel {
    var items: [CartItem] = []
    var couponCode: String = ""
}

struct CartHeader: View {
    var model: CartModel
    var body: some View {
        // reads only items.count -> invalidated only when items change
        Text("Items: \(model.items.count)")
    }
}

struct CouponField: View {
    @Bindable var model: CartModel
    var body: some View {
        // reads only couponCode -> typing does NOT re-run CartHeader.body
        TextField("Coupon", text: $model.couponCode)
    }
}
class CartViewModel : ViewModel() {
    val items = MutableStateFlow<List<CartItem>>(emptyList())
    val couponCode = MutableStateFlow("")
}

@Composable
fun CartHeader(items: List<CartItem>) {      // takes only what it needs
    Text("Items: ${items.size}")
}

@Composable
fun CouponField(code: String, onChange: (String) -> Unit) {
    TextField(value = code, onValueChange = onChange)
}

With the legacy ObservableObject pattern (old codebases), any @Published change fires objectWillChange and every view observing that object re-evaluates its body, even if it read none of the changed properties. This is a classic over-invalidation source and a reason many teams migrated to @Observable. Compose users know the analogue: passing a whole UiState to every composable.

Important truths:

  • Re-running body is not re-rendering. Cheap bodies that produce an identical tree cause little GPU work, but they still consume main-thread CPU.
  • body must be a pure, fast function of state. No sorting 10k items, no date formatting with a fresh DateFormatter each call, no I/O.
  • Parent invalidation: when a parent's body runs, children structs are recreated; SwiftUI re-evaluates child bodies unless it can prove inputs are unchanged. Children whose stored properties are all Equatable-comparable (plain value data) can be skipped by SwiftUI's automatic comparison for views with POD-like storage; closures and reference types defeat the comparison. This is like Compose's stability: a lambda that captures changing state is a "new" input every time. Verify exact diffing rules; Apple documents behaviour loosely.
  • Debug with let _ = Self._printChanges() inside body (a debugging-only API) to print what triggered a re-evaluation.
var body: some View {
    let _ = Self._printChanges()   // prints "@self, @identity, _count changed." in the console; debug only
    Text("\(count)")
}

Real examples. Point-Free's Swift Composable Architecture uses Store scoping and ViewStore/observation to limit invalidation, a response to exactly this problem. Many teams moved big screens from ObservableObject view models to @Observable and saw drops in body evaluations in the SwiftUI instrument.

Analogy. A spreadsheet: change one cell and only formulas that read it recalculate. ObservableObject was like recalculating the whole sheet whenever any cell changed; @Observable tracks each formula's precedents.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying SwiftUI "redraws the whole screen" on every state change. It re-evaluates affected bodies and diffs.
  • Believing body is called once per frame. It is called when dependencies change, which may be hundreds of times during a drag if you bind state to a gesture without care.
  • Putting a heavy ForEach filter inside body rather than precomputing in the model.
  • Android vs iOS: assuming a lambda parameter is stable. A closure capturing mutable state looks different each time and blocks skipping.

notes.title: View identity, equatable views and avoiding expensive bodies
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Compose uses key() and positional memoization; LazyColumn(key = ...) keeps item state stable. SwiftUI uses identity: either structural (position in the view tree) or explicit (.id(_:) or ForEach identifiers).

Why identity matters for performance and correctness:

  • Same identity across updates means SwiftUI updates the existing node and preserves its @State. Changed identity means it destroys and recreates the node, losing state and re-running onAppear, often with animation glitches.
  • ForEach over data needs stable Identifiable IDs. Using \.self on mutable values or UUID() generated inside body creates new identities on every pass, so the whole list is rebuilt:
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// BAD: new identity each evaluation
ForEach(items.map { Row(id: UUID(), title: $0.title) }) { RowView(row: $0) }

// GOOD: stable identity from the model
ForEach(items) { item in RowView(item: item) }   // item: Identifiable with stable id
// BAD: no key, items matched by position
items(items) { RowView(it) }

// GOOD: stable key
items(items, key = { it.id }) { RowView(it) }
  • Conditional views with if produce different structural identities for each branch (_ConditionalContent), so state inside is reset when the branch flips. Prefer modifiers like .opacity(0) or .hidden() when you need to keep state, or use .id deliberately to force a reset.
  • AnyView type-erases and defeats diffing optimisations; use @ViewBuilder, generics or Group instead. WWDC talks ("Demystify SwiftUI", WWDC21) cover identity, lifetime and dependencies.

Taming expensive bodies:

  1. Extract subviews. Splitting a large body into smaller structs gives SwiftUI smaller invalidation units. A computed property returning some View inside the same struct is NOT a separate unit; it re-evaluates with the parent.
  2. Precompute. Do sorting/filtering in the model (or a cached computed property) rather than in body.
  3. Cache formatters. DateFormatter, NumberFormatter and ByteCountFormatter are expensive to create. Use static instances or the modern FormatStyle (.formatted(.dateTime...)).
  4. EquatableView / .equatable(). For a view whose inputs are Equatable, .equatable() makes SwiftUI skip body when inputs compare equal:
struct PriceChart: View, Equatable {
    let points: [Double]
    var body: some View { /* expensive Canvas drawing */ Canvas { _, _ in } }
}
// use: PriceChart(points: pts).equatable()
  1. drawingGroup() flattens a complex subtree to a Metal-rendered offscreen bitmap; it helps for many overlapping vector layers but can hurt simple views and text quality. Measure.
  2. Avoid GeometryReader in lists and nested loops; it forces extra layout passes and frame reads.
  3. Prefer lazy containers (LazyVStack, List) for large collections; plain VStack inside ScrollView instantiates all children eagerly.
struct FeedScreen: View {
    let items: [FeedItem]
    var body: some View {
        ScrollView {
            LazyVStack(spacing: 12) {          // creates rows as they approach the viewport
                ForEach(items) { FeedRow(item: $0) }
            }
        }
    }
}

List on iOS 16+ is backed by UICollectionView and reuses cells, so it handles very large datasets better than LazyVStack, which keeps created views alive once built (memory grows as you scroll; verify current behaviour as it has changed between releases).

Real examples. Teams at Airbnb and Lyft report replacing AnyView usage and splitting monolithic bodies when moving to SwiftUI; the SwiftUI instrument's "View Body" lane highlights which views evaluate and how long each takes.

Analogy. Name tags at a conference: if you give attendees new name tags every minute, the host cannot recognise them and re-registers everyone; stable tags mean only people who changed are updated.

Common interview traps.

  • Using id: \.self for structs with changing fields, or generating UUID() in body.
  • Believing a some View computed property is a separate view for diffing purposes.
  • Sprinkling AnyView for convenience and losing diffing.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting remember semantics; SwiftUI state persistence is tied to identity, not position alone.

notes.title: Scrolling performance and image loading
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Coil, Glide and Picasso decode and cache images, downsample to the target view size, and cancel loads when views recycle. In iOS: Nuke, Kingfisher, SDWebImage, and SwiftUI's built-in AsyncImage.

The cost model: a 12 MP JPEG (4032 x 3024) decodes to roughly width * height * 4 bytes = about 48.8 MB of bitmap memory, regardless of its file size, because decoded bitmaps are 4 bytes per pixel (RGBA). Showing that in a 100 pt thumbnail wastes enormous memory and decode time. This applies identically on Android with Bitmaps.

Decoding location matters: UIImage(data:) creates a lightweight object; the actual decode is lazy and often happens on the main thread at first draw, producing hitches during scroll. The fix is to decode off the main thread, at the target size.

Downsampling with ImageIO (the recommended approach, WWDC18 "Image and Graphics Best Practices"):

import ImageIO
import UIKit

func downsample(data: Data, to pointSize: CGSize, scale: CGFloat) -> UIImage? {
    let srcOptions = [kCGImageSourceShouldCache: false] as CFDictionary
    guard let source = CGImageSourceCreateWithData(data as CFData, srcOptions) else { return nil }

    let maxDimension = max(pointSize.width, pointSize.height) * scale
    let options = [
        kCGImageSourceCreateThumbnailFromImageAlways: true,
        kCGImageSourceShouldCacheImmediately: true,      // decode now, on this (background) thread
        kCGImageSourceCreateThumbnailWithTransform: true,
        kCGImageSourceThumbnailMaxPixelSize: maxDimension
    ] as CFDictionary

    guard let cg = CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex(source, 0, options) else { return nil }
    return UIImage(cgImage: cg)
}

UIImage.preparingThumbnail(of:) and byPreparingThumbnail(ofSize:) (iOS 15+) offer a simpler API, with async variants, that decodes off the main thread; verify exact names in current docs.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func thumbnail(for data: Data) async -> UIImage? {
    guard let image = UIImage(data: data) else { return nil }
    return await image.byPreparingThumbnail(ofSize: CGSize(width: 200, height: 200))
}
suspend fun thumbnail(bytes: ByteArray): Bitmap = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    val opts = BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inSampleSize = 4 }
    BitmapFactory.decodeByteArray(bytes, 0, bytes.size, opts)
}

AsyncImage (iOS 15+) is convenient but limited: it uses the shared URLCache for HTTP caching but offers no controllable in-memory image cache or downsampling, reload behaviour inside lists can flicker, and cancellation depends on view lifetime. Fine for prototypes and small screens; for feeds teams use Nuke (with LazyImage) or Kingfisher (KFImage) that provide memory plus disk caches, prefetching, downsampling processors and request de-duplication.

Caching layers:

  • Memory cache: NSCache (auto-evicts under pressure, thread-safe, does not copy keys). Not a Dictionary that grows forever.
  • Disk cache: URLCache for HTTP semantics, or the library's own disk store.
  • HTTP caching: honour Cache-Control/ETag; configure URLSession with a sized URLCache (the default shared cache is small).

Other scroll-performance rules:

  • Avoid layer effects that force off-screen rendering (shadow + corner radius on many cells). In SwiftUI, .shadow on every row of a long list is costly; pre-render or simplify.
  • Avoid large blur/material stacks in rows.
  • Use fixed or cheaply computed row heights where possible. Self-sizing is fine but expensive with complex Auto Layout.
  • Cancel image tasks when rows disappear (onDisappear or the library's built-in handling). Without cancellation, fast scrolling queues hundreds of loads.
  • Prefetch with UICollectionViewDataSourcePrefetching (UIKit) or the library's ImagePrefetcher / ImagePrefetcher equivalents in Nuke/Kingfisher.
  • Use .task(id:) for async loads tied to a row identity, which cancels automatically when the row leaves:
struct Avatar: View {
    let url: URL
    @State private var image: UIImage?

    var body: some View {
        Group {
            if let image { Image(uiImage: image).resizable() } else { Color.gray.opacity(0.2) }
        }
        .frame(width: 44, height: 44)
        .clipShape(Circle())
        .task(id: url) {                       // cancelled automatically if row disappears or url changes
            image = await ImagePipeline.shared.thumbnail(url, size: 44)  // your own wrapper, not an Apple API
        }
    }
}

Real examples. Instagram and Pinterest invest heavily in image pipelines (progressive JPEG, prefetch, downsampling). Nuke is known for fast pipelines and Swift concurrency support; Kingfisher is widely adopted in SwiftUI and UIKit apps.

Analogy. Shipping photos for an album: you shrink prints to the album's size before putting them in the box, rather than mailing poster-size enlargements and trimming at the destination.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing file size equals memory size; decoded bitmaps are width x height x 4 bytes.
  • Using AsyncImage in a long feed and calling it production-ready.
  • Doing UIImage(data:) then assigning on the main thread and expecting no hitch because "it's just one line".
  • Using a Dictionary as an image cache with no eviction, which causes memory-warning kills (jetsam).

notes.title: Memory: ARC, leaks and Instruments Allocations
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Android has a garbage collector, OutOfMemoryError, LeakCanary and the Memory Profiler heap dump. iOS uses ARC (compile-time inserted retain/release; no GC), with the Jetsam daemon killing apps that exceed memory limits.

Key facts:

  • Each class instance has a reference count. When it hits zero, deinit runs and memory is freed deterministically (no GC pauses).
  • Cycles are never collected. A closure property capturing self strongly, with self owning the closure, leaks both. Use [weak self] (optional) or [unowned self] (crash if freed; use only when lifetimes are guaranteed).
  • Structs and enums do not have reference counts themselves, but they can contain references (a struct holding a class instance retains it when copied). Copying a large struct with many reference fields causes many retains.
  • iOS has no swap file for app memory. Under pressure the system sends memory warnings, then jetsam terminates background apps, and eventually the foreground one. The footprint limit varies by device RAM and OS; do not hardcode numbers (verify per device from Organizer/MetricKit data). A jetsam kill leaves no normal crash log; it appears under "Memory" terminations in Organizer or as EXC_RESOURCE/jetsam event reports in device logs.

Typical leak sources:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
final class FeedViewModel {
    var onUpdate: (() -> Void)?
    private var timer: Timer?

    func start() {
        // LEAK: Timer retains target closure; closure retains self; self retains timer
        timer = Timer.scheduledTimer(withTimeInterval: 1, repeats: true) { _ in
            self.refresh()
        }
    }
    // FIX: [weak self] and invalidate in a stop() called from viewDidDisappear / onDisappear
}
class FeedViewModel {
    private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
    // Android leak: a Runnable holding the Activity; GC handles pure cycles,
    // but static/long-lived references still leak (LeakCanary finds them)
}

Other classic leaks: NotificationCenter block observers capturing self strongly (the center holds the block), Combine sink capturing self strongly while storing AnyCancellable in self (a cycle), delegates declared strong, Task { self.work() } stored forever (long-lived tasks hold self; cancel them), and URLSession delegates (the session retains its delegate until invalidated).

Tools and workflow:

  1. Debug Memory Graph (Xcode, the three-circle button): shows live objects and retain relationships; enable "Malloc Stack" (scheme diagnostics) to see allocation backtraces. The purple "!" marks detected leaks.
  2. Instruments > Allocations: use "Mark Generation" before and after navigating to a screen and back; growth between generations that should be zero indicates leaks (persistent allocations). Filter by your type name (e.g. ProfileViewController).
  3. Instruments > Leaks: detects unreachable cycles; won't find memory that is reachable but unnecessary (e.g. an unbounded cache).
  4. deinit logging and unit tests asserting deallocation using weak references:
@Test func viewModelDeallocates() async {
    weak var weakVM: FeedViewModel?
    do {
        let vm = FeedViewModel()
        weakVM = vm
        vm.start()
        vm.stop()
    }
    #expect(weakVM == nil)
}
  1. VM Tracker shows dirty/resident/swapped memory; image buffers appear under "IOSurface" or "CG image" regions.

Memory reduction levers: downsample images (previous section), use NSCache, release large buffers on UIApplication.didReceiveMemoryWarningNotification (or didReceiveMemoryWarning), avoid holding full result sets (page them), and prefer value semantics carefully (copy-on-write for arrays means mutation of a shared buffer triggers a copy).

Real examples. Facebook famously built FBRetainCycleDetector for iOS because cycles were common in a huge codebase. Sentry and Firebase Crashlytics now report out-of-memory terminations heuristically (OOM detection is inferred, not directly reported by iOS).

Analogy. Library books with check-out counts: when the last borrower returns it (count zero), the book goes back immediately. Two friends who each refuse to return a book until the other does keep it forever; that is a retain cycle.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "use weak everywhere"; weak breaks needed ownership and unowned crashes after dealloc.
  • Believing Leaks finds everything; it misses reachable-but-unbounded growth ("abandoned memory").
  • Assuming Task {} inside a view model is auto-cancelled with the object.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting GC to resolve cycles; also expecting a stable OOM exception: iOS silently kills you.

notes.title: Instruments toolkit: Time Profiler, SwiftUI, Hangs and more
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Android Studio Profiler plus Perfetto traces. Instruments is a separate app (Xcode > Open Developer Tool > Instruments, or Product > Profile with Cmd+I), with templates composed of "instruments" recording on a shared timeline.

Golden rules:

  • Profile a Release build (Cmd+I builds with the Profile scheme, Release by default) on a real device, preferably the oldest supported one. Simulators run on Mac CPU/GPU and hide real hitches.
  • Record a short, focused scenario (scroll one list for 10 seconds), not the whole app session.
  • Compare before and after with the same steps.

Key templates:

Instrument Use it for What you look at
Time Profiler CPU hotspots Call tree; check "Hide System Libraries", "Invert Call Tree", "Separate by Thread" (main thread first)
Hangs Main thread stalls Hang intervals with durations and stack at the time
Animation Hitches Dropped frames Hitch intervals with commit/render breakdown
SwiftUI (Xcode 16 template) View body evaluation counts, causes of updates "View Body", "View Properties", "Update Groups" lanes; verify lane names for your Xcode
Allocations Memory growth Generations, persistent bytes, allocation backtraces
Leaks Retain cycles Leaked objects with reference graph
Network Request timing Per-request latency and payload
Energy Log / Power Profiler Battery impact CPU, network, location, GPU activity
System Trace Thread scheduling, priority inversion, locks Thread states, run queue
File Activity / Disk I/O in launch or scroll Syscalls on main thread
App Launch Launch phases dyld, static initialisers, first frame

Reading Time Profiler:

  1. Select the main thread and the time range of the hitch.
  2. Invert the call tree to see heaviest leaf functions by self time.
  3. Hide system libraries to see your symbols; then re-enable to see if the cost is inside SwiftUI/UIKit (usually meaning you triggered too much work).
  4. Double-click a frame to jump to source; look for JSON decoding, String operations on huge text, DateFormatter creation, sorting, synchronous disk reads.

Reading SwiftUI instrument: it shows how many times each body ran and the cause of the update (which state changed). A body running 200 times in a one-second scroll is a signal; the cause trace reveals a binding updated on every scroll offset change.

Signposts let you mark your own intervals so they show in Instruments:

import os

private let signposter = OSSignposter(subsystem: "com.example.app", category: "feed")

func loadFeed() async throws {
    let state = signposter.beginInterval("loadFeed")
    defer { signposter.endInterval("loadFeed", state) }
    try await repository.refresh()
}

Main Thread Checker (on by default in Xcode debug runs) warns about UI API calls from background threads. Thread Sanitizer and Swift 6 strict concurrency find data races. For automated regression guards, XCTest still provides XCTMetric performance tests (measure(metrics: [XCTClockMetric(), XCTMemoryMetric()])), which Swift Testing does not replace yet (verify current state); this is a place where XCTest remains the right tool.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func testScrollPerformance() throws {
    let app = XCUIApplication()
    app.launch()
    measure(metrics: [XCTOSSignpostMetric.scrollDecelerationMetric]) {
        app.tables.firstMatch.swipeUp(velocity: .fast)
    }
}
@get:Rule val benchmarkRule = MacrobenchmarkRule()

@Test fun scroll() = benchmarkRule.measureRepeated(
    packageName = "com.example.app",
    metrics = listOf(FrameTimingMetric()),
    iterations = 5,
    startupMode = StartupMode.WARM
) {
    device.findObject(By.res("feed")).fling(Direction.DOWN)
}

Real examples. Uber and Meta describe running automated scroll-hitch tests in CI with XCTest metrics and flagging regressions; Apple's own WWDC sessions ("Analyze hangs with Instruments", "Explore UI animation hitches") demonstrate the Hangs and Hitches instruments.

Analogy. Instruments is a flight data recorder with separate channels (engine, altitude, fuel); you replay the same flight and look at which channel misbehaved at the moment of the bump.

Common interview traps.

  • Profiling a debug build on the simulator and drawing conclusions.
  • Staring at the whole-run call tree instead of selecting the hitch interval.
  • Not knowing the difference between a hang (unresponsive) and a hitch (dropped frames).
  • Android vs iOS: expecting one tool for all; Instruments templates are separate recordings that you often combine.

notes.title: Main thread hangs and structured concurrency for responsiveness
notes.html:
Android equivalent. ANR (Application Not Responding) after 5 seconds of input blocking, StrictMode to catch disk/network on main, Dispatchers.Main vs Default/IO. In iOS: @MainActor, Task.detached, nonisolated async functions and the Hangs instrument. iOS does not show a user ANR dialog; it just feels frozen, and the user force-quits. The watchdog only kills for launch, resume and certain background-transition time limits.

Common hang sources:

  • Synchronous disk or Keychain access on the main thread (Keychain calls can take many milliseconds).
  • JSON decoding of big payloads in a @MainActor view model.
  • Core Data or SwiftData fetches on the main context with huge result sets.
  • DispatchQueue.main.sync from background code, or sync onto a queue that is blocked (deadlock).
  • Large body computations (see earlier).
  • Synchronous image decode.

In Swift 6, concurrency rules help: a function marked @MainActor runs on the main thread; a plain async function that is nonisolated runs on the global concurrent executor (in Swift 6.0 semantics; Swift 6.2's "approachable concurrency" setting NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault changes where nonisolated async functions run, so verify your project settings).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor
@Observable
final class FeedViewModel {
    private(set) var items: [FeedItem] = []
    private let repository: FeedRepository

    init(repository: FeedRepository) { self.repository = repository }

    func refresh() async {
        // Heavy work happens off the main actor inside the repository (an actor or nonisolated async function)
        let loaded = (try? await repository.loadAndParse()) ?? []
        items = loaded      // back on the main actor automatically
    }
}

actor FeedRepository {
    func loadAndParse() async throws -> [FeedItem] {
        let (data, _) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: feedURL)
        return try JSONDecoder().decode([FeedItem].self, from: data)   // CPU work runs on the actor's executor, not main
    }
}
class FeedViewModel(private val repository: FeedRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _items = MutableStateFlow<List<FeedItem>>(emptyList())
    val items = _items.asStateFlow()

    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {                  // Main by default
        _items.value = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {   // heavy work off main
            repository.loadAndParse()
        }
    }
}

Careful: a call from @MainActor to an actor method awaits and hops; the heavy work runs on the actor's executor. A @MainActor method that does a loop of CPU work runs entirely on the main thread even if it is async; async alone does not mean background.

Other responsiveness tips:

  • Debounce rapid input (search) with .task(id:) plus try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300)); cancellation of the previous task makes it a debounce.
  • Move disk-heavy SwiftData work to a ModelActor (background context).
  • Batch UI updates; avoid updating @Observable state per row of a progress loop thousands of times per second.
  • Use os_signpost to find which phase blocks.

Hangs in the field: Xcode Organizer > Hang Rate (and MetricKit MXHangDiagnostic) shows call stacks aggregated across users; this is how you find hangs that never reproduce locally (e.g. slow older devices, large user data sets).

Real examples. Instagram and Facebook track "hang rate" as a core metric; a classic fix pattern is moving feed parsing and image decode off the main thread and capping main-thread work per frame.

Analogy. A cashier who also has to restock shelves: customers queue while she restocks. Hiring a stock clerk (background work) keeps the till moving.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing async means background; actor isolation decides where code runs.
  • Using DispatchQueue.main.sync and deadlocking.
  • Marking everything @MainActor for convenience and then doing heavy parsing there.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting an ANR dialog; the failure mode is silent freezing or watchdog termination during launch.

notes.title: Launch time optimisation
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Cold start, App Startup library, Baseline Profiles, reportFullyDrawn, and the Play Console cold-start vitals. iOS has "cold" (no process, not recently launched), "warm" and "resume" launches, and Apple's guidance is to aim for a first frame in under about 400 ms after the user taps the icon (Apple's WWDC talks cite roughly 400 ms to complete launch; verify the figure).

Launch phases:

tap icon
  |
  v
[pre-main]  kernel exec -> dyld loads dylibs/frameworks -> rebases/binds -> ObjC runtime setup
            -> static initialisers (+load, C++ globals) 
  |
  v
[main -> first frame]  UIApplicationMain / @main -> App init -> scene -> first view body -> first CA commit
  |
  v
[post-launch]  fully interactive, data loaded (you define this; use os_signpost)

Pre-main optimisations (see Apple WWDC22 "Link fast: Improve build and launch times"):

  • Fewer dynamic frameworks. Each dynamic framework costs dyld work. Prefer static linking for your own SPM modules and third-party libraries where possible; mergeable libraries (Xcode 15+) let you keep dynamic in debug and merge in release. Use fewer than a handful of dynamic frameworks if you can.
  • Remove +load methods in Objective-C and heavy static initialisers. Avoid doing work in global let constants that initialise before first use (Swift globals are lazy, but Obj-C +load and C++ constructors are not).
  • Reduce binary size and Objective-C classes where reasonable; dead-strip unused code and keep Strip Linking Dead Code enabled in Release.
  • Avoid third-party SDK initialisation in didFinishLaunching that does network or disk work: analytics, crash reporters, A/B SDKs, ad SDKs commonly add 100s of ms combined.

Post-main optimisations:

  • Defer non-essential initialisation until after the first frame:
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@main
struct ShopApp: App {
    @State private var model = AppModel()          // keep init cheap

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            RootView()
                .environment(model)
                .task {                              // runs after the first view appears
                    await model.warmUpSecondaryServices()   // analytics, remote config, prefetch
                }
        }
    }
}
class ShopApp : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        // Use App Startup / lazy init; defer analytics, remote config
        CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default).launch { warmUpSecondaryServices() }
    }
}
  • Show cached content immediately (stale-while-revalidate) rather than blocking the first screen on the network.
  • Keep the launch screen static (UILaunchScreen in Info.plist or a storyboard); it is not an animated splash. Apple's HIG discourages splash branding and fake delays.
  • Avoid synchronous Keychain reads, large UserDefaults plists, database migrations and Core Data/SwiftData container setup on the main thread before first frame; run migrations lazily or off main where safe.
  • Reduce first-screen view complexity: a LazyVStack of placeholders is cheaper than a fully populated complex screen.
  • Prewarming: since iOS 15 the system may prewarm your app (run pre-main work in advance). That makes naive "time to main()" measurements in production misleading; use ProcessInfo / NSProcessInfoPrewarm-aware logic (the ActivePrewarm environment variable), and measure to the first rendered frame instead. Verify details on prewarm detection.

Measuring:

  • Instruments > App Launch template shows phase breakdown.
  • Xcode Organizer > Launch Time aggregates real-user percentiles per version.
  • DYLD_PRINT_STATISTICS=1 (old dyld; verify applicability on modern iOS) printed pre-main time in the legacy days.
  • MetricKit MXAppLaunchMetric gives histograms of time-to-first-draw and resume time.
  • Custom signposts from main to first onAppear of the root view.

Watchdog: if launching exceeds the system limit (long synchronous work in didFinishLaunching), the app is killed with 0x8badf00d. Typical cause: synchronous network call or lock wait on launch; fix by deferring.

Real examples. Uber, Facebook and Spotify engineering blogs describe cutting launch time by converting dynamic frameworks to static, trimming initialisers, and measuring "time to first meaningful content" as a product metric. Pinterest reported using startup task graphs (dependency ordered, off-main).

Analogy. Opening a shop in the morning: lights and till first (first frame), then restock shelves and print flyers while customers already walk in.

Common interview traps.

  • Measuring only main() time and ignoring first-frame time.
  • Adding yet another dynamic framework per feature.
  • Doing SDK initialisation synchronously in didFinishLaunching.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting Baseline Profiles; native iOS code is already AOT-compiled, so the levers are dyld work and main-thread init work.

notes.title: MetricKit and Xcode Organizer
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Play Console Android Vitals (ANR rate, crash rate, startup, slow frames, battery wakelocks) and Firebase Performance. In iOS, Xcode Organizer shows aggregated, privacy-preserving data from users who opted in to share analytics; MetricKit delivers on-device aggregated payloads to your own code so you can upload them to your backend.

Organizer (Window > Organizer) tabs: Crashes, Energy, Disk Writes, Hangs, Launch Time, Memory, Terminations, Scrolling (hitch rate), Battery Usage. You compare versions and device models, and drill into top call stacks with symbolication (needs dSYMs/bitcode-free builds uploaded to App Store Connect, automatic for App Store builds).

MetricKit usage:

import MetricKit

final class MetricsSubscriber: NSObject, MXMetricManagerSubscriber {
    override init() {
        super.init()
        MXMetricManager.shared.add(self)
    }

    deinit { MXMetricManager.shared.remove(self) }

    // Daily aggregated metrics (about once per 24 hours)
    func didReceive(_ payloads: [MXMetricPayload]) {
        for payload in payloads {
            let json = payload.jsonRepresentation()          // Data
            upload(json)
        }
    }

    // Diagnostics: crashes, hangs, CPU exceptions, disk write exceptions (iOS 14+ for MXDiagnosticPayload; iOS 15+ hangs; verify)
    func didReceive(_ payloads: [MXDiagnosticPayload]) {
        for payload in payloads {
            upload(payload.jsonRepresentation())
        }
    }

    private func upload(_ data: Data) { /* send to your backend */ }
}

What the payloads include: launch and resume histograms (MXAppLaunchMetric), hang time (MXAppResponsivenessMetric), CPU and GPU time, memory peak (MXMemoryMetric), disk writes, cellular and Wi-Fi bytes, animation hitch ratios (MXAnimationMetric), exit reasons (MXAppExitMetric: normal, watchdog, memory-resource limit, background task timeout, etc.).

Custom metrics: wrap your code with mxSignpost using MXMetricManager.makeLogHandle(category:) and signpost intervals; they appear in daily payloads as MXSignpostMetric aggregates (verify the exact API shape).

let log = MXMetricManager.makeLogHandle(category: "checkout")

func checkout() async {
    mxSignpost(.begin, log: log, name: "checkout")
    defer { mxSignpost(.end, log: log, name: "checkout") }
    await performCheckout()
}

Practical points:

  • Payloads arrive at most once a day, delayed; MetricKit is for trends, not live debugging.
  • Combine with a third-party crash reporter (Sentry, Firebase Crashlytics, Datadog RUM) for real-time alerts. Sentry also offers app-hang detection and performance tracing on top.
  • Not available in the Simulator for real payload delivery (use Xcode's Debug > Simulate MetricKit Payloads).
  • Respect privacy: payloads are aggregated and contain no user identifiers, but your upload still counts as data collection for App Privacy labels if combined with identifiers.

Real examples. Large apps set release gates such as "hang rate must not regress by more than X percent" using Organizer or in-house dashboards built from MetricKit payloads (the specific thresholds are team-defined, not Apple-defined).

Analogy. MetricKit is the black box that mails you a monthly flight summary; Organizer is the airline's industry safety report across all customers.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting MetricKit to deliver instantly or in the simulator.
  • Forgetting dSYMs so call stacks are unsymbolicated.
  • Treating Organizer data as complete; it only covers users who share diagnostics.
  • Android vs iOS: Play Vitals are automatic for every Play-installed user; Organizer depends on opt-in.

notes.title: Battery, energy and thermal behaviour
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Doze, App Standby buckets, WorkManager constraints, wake locks, Battery Historian and Android Vitals "excessive wakeups". In iOS the big levers are background execution limits, location accuracy, networking radio use, CPU/GPU load and thermal state.

Energy drains to know:

  • CPU/GPU work: continuous animations, TimelineView(.animation) or CADisplayLink running when nothing changes, un-throttled polling, complex blurs.
  • Networking: frequent small requests keep the cellular radio in a high-power state. Batch requests, use URLSession background sessions with isDiscretionary for non-urgent transfers, enable HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection reuse, and use push notifications (APNs) rather than polling.
  • Location: continuous GPS is costly. Use the lowest desiredAccuracy that works, significant-change or visit monitoring, and stop updates when done. Since iOS 17 CLLocationUpdate.liveUpdates() async API exists (verify); also CLMonitor (iOS 17).
  • Bluetooth, camera, microphone: stop sessions when not visible.
  • Timers: prefer coalescable timers with tolerance; avoid sub-second repeating timers on the main run loop in background.
  • Background work: BGTaskScheduler with BGAppRefreshTask and BGProcessingTask lets the system run work at good times; there is no guarantee of when. Silent pushes are throttled by the system.
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func scheduleRefresh() {
    let request = BGAppRefreshTaskRequest(identifier: "com.example.app.refresh")
    request.earliestBeginDate = Date(timeIntervalSinceNow: 15 * 60)   // a hint only
    try? BGTaskScheduler.shared.submit(request)
}
val request = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<RefreshWorker>(15, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
    .setConstraints(Constraints.Builder().setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED).build())
    .build()
WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueueUniquePeriodicWork("refresh", ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP, request)

Thermal state: ProcessInfo.processInfo.thermalState returns .nominal, .fair, .serious, .critical; observe ProcessInfo.thermalStateDidChangeNotification and reduce work (lower frame rate, quality, pause prefetch) at .serious. Also check ProcessInfo.processInfo.isLowPowerModeEnabled and NSProcessInfoPowerStateDidChange to disable autoplay, background refresh and heavy animations.

func adaptQuality() {
    let info = ProcessInfo.processInfo
    if info.thermalState.rawValue >= ProcessInfo.ThermalState.serious.rawValue || info.isLowPowerModeEnabled {
        videoPlayer.preferredMaximumResolution = CGSize(width: 960, height: 540)
    }
}

Measuring energy: Xcode debug gauge for Energy Impact (coarse), Instruments Power Profiler (iOS 16+ template; verify name), Organizer Energy tab, MetricKit CPU/GPU/location/network counters. Test on a real device unplugged; Xcode's gauge is a rough index, not milliamps.

Common production incident: a screen leaves a CADisplayLink or Timer running after dismissal, causing CPU use and heat in the background; a second pattern is a location manager left in continuous updates after logout.

Real examples. Uber and Lyft reduce location update frequency when the app is backgrounded or when the driver is idle; Spotify limits background activity and prefetch on low battery; video apps adapt bitrate on thermal pressure.

Analogy. A phone is like a car on a hot day: flooring the accelerator (CPU) while the air conditioner (radio) runs full blast overheats the engine; the car's computer (iOS) then forces you to slow down.

Common interview traps.

  • Polling every few seconds instead of using push or background sessions.
  • Assuming BGTaskScheduler runs at the requested time; it is best effort.
  • Forgetting to stop CADisplayLink, timers, location and audio sessions on teardown.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting WorkManager-style guaranteed execution; iOS background execution is far more limited and opportunistic.

notes.title: Performance review checklist and interview answers
notes.html:
Android equivalent. The "jank triage" playbook: reproduce, capture a trace, find the long frame, find the owning code, fix, verify with a benchmark.

A repeatable approach to "this screen is janky":

  1. Reproduce on a real, older device with a Release build.
  2. Classify: hang (main thread blocked), hitch (frames late), memory (growth or jetsam), launch, or battery.
  3. Capture: Animation Hitches/Hangs for stutter, Time Profiler for CPU, SwiftUI instrument for excess body evaluations, Allocations for memory.
  4. Locate: the heaviest main-thread function, the view whose body repeats, the allocation growing per scroll.
  5. Fix with the cheapest correct lever (below).
  6. Verify with the same recording, then add a guard (an XCTMetric test, a signpost, or a dashboard alert).

Lever cheat sheet:

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Whole screen re-evaluates on typing Shared ObservableObject / one big observable read everywhere Use @Observable, split views, pass only needed values
Stutter while scrolling images Main-thread decode, full-size bitmaps Downsample off main, Nuke/Kingfisher, prefetch
State resets when scrolling or toggling Identity change Stable id, avoid if branches that swap structure
Rows redraw all at once VStack in ScrollView LazyVStack or List
Slow launch Many dynamic frameworks, eager SDK init Static link, defer init, show cached content
Memory climbs per screen visit Retain cycle Memory graph, [weak self], cancel Tasks
Phone gets hot Timer/DisplayLink/location left running Tear down in onDisappear/deinit
Random freeze Sync I/O or main.sync Move to actor/background, avoid sync

Sample interview answers (senior tone):

  • "How would you debug a janky list?" Profile in Instruments on device in Release. Check Hitches for commit vs render cost, Time Profiler for main-thread hot paths (decode, formatters), SwiftUI instrument for body counts. Fix identity, lazy containers, downsampling, cached formatters; verify with an XCTMetric scroll test.
  • "SwiftUI vs UIKit performance?" Both can be smooth; SwiftUI's cost is body evaluation and diffing, UIKit's is Auto Layout and view allocation. SwiftUI lists have improved since List moved onto UICollectionView; for extreme cases (huge lists, complex custom layouts) some teams still drop to UIKit with UIHostingConfiguration for cell content.
  • "What causes memory warnings and how do you handle them?" Large images, unbounded caches, retain cycles. Downsample, use NSCache, release on warning, profile Allocations and Memory Graph.
  • "How do you reduce app launch?" Measure phases; cut dynamic frameworks, move SDK init after first frame, avoid sync I/O, render cached UI.

Verify list for this topic: exact hang thresholds, SwiftUI instrument lane names in Xcode 16/26, byPreparingThumbnail signature, MetricKit signpost API shape, Power Profiler template name, CLLocationUpdate/CLMonitor availability, Swift 6.2 default isolation settings.

Analogy. Diagnosing a slow car: you do not replace parts at random; you connect the diagnostic computer, read the fault code, fix that part, and run the same test drive again.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to fixes before measuring, or claiming a fix without a before/after trace.
  • Proposing UIKit rewrites for a problem caused by a single AnyView/identity bug.
  • Ignoring older devices and low-power mode when judging results.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Performance work on iOS means Release builds on real devices, measured with Instruments, Organizer and MetricKit; frame budget is about 16.7 ms (8.3 ms at 120 Hz).
  • SwiftUI re-runs body when a read dependency changes; @Observable tracks per-property reads and reduces over-invalidation versus legacy ObservableObject.
  • Stable identity, small subviews, precomputed data, cached formatters, .equatable(), lazy containers and avoiding AnyView keep bodies cheap.
  • Images: decoded size is width x height x 4 bytes; downsample off the main thread, use Nuke/Kingfisher over AsyncImage in feeds, cache with NSCache and URLCache, cancel on disappearance.
  • Memory: ARC does not collect cycles; use [weak self], cancel Tasks, check with Debug Memory Graph and Allocations generations; jetsam kills silently.
  • Instruments templates (Time Profiler, Hangs, Hitches, SwiftUI, Allocations, Leaks, System Trace, App Launch) are used with focused scenarios; add os_signpost.
  • Responsiveness: async is not background; isolate heavy work in actors or nonisolated functions and keep @MainActor for state.
  • Launch: reduce dynamic frameworks and static initialisers, defer SDK init, show cached UI, mind prewarming, avoid watchdog 0x8badf00d.
  • Battery: batch networking, lower location accuracy, stop timers and display links, observe thermal state and Low Power Mode.
  • Items marked verify: hang thresholds, SwiftUI instrument lanes, thumbnail API names, MetricKit signpost shape, Power Profiler naming, Swift 6.2 isolation defaults.
